blocks.content: Every algorithm covered so far in this module, FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Priority Scheduling, and Round Robin, answers the same underlying question: which process should the CPU run next. Preemptive versus non-preemptive answers a completely different question, one that sits underneath all of them. Once the CPU has been handed to a process, can the operating system take it back before that process is finished? This is not a sixth scheduling algorithm sitting alongside the other five. It is a property, the single most important dividing line in this entire module, and every algorithm you have already learned falls cleanly on one side of it or the other.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to state, without hesitation, whether each algorithm in this module is preemptive or non-preemptive and why. You will know exactly what event triggers a preemption, what real tradeoffs the two approaches make, and why nearly every general purpose operating system in the world commits to preemptive scheduling despite its extra complexity.
1. A Property, Not a Sixth Algorithm
blocks.text: 1. A Property, Not a Sixth Algorithm

blocks.content: It is tempting to treat preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling as just another pair of algorithms to memorize, the way you memorized FCFS or Round Robin. That framing is wrong and it will hurt you in an interview. Preemptive and non-preemptive are not algorithms at all. They are a classification, a lens you place over an algorithm to describe one specific behavior it exhibits: what happens to a running process when something more important shows up.

blocks.title: The one question this chapter answers
blocks.content: Can the operating system forcibly take the CPU away from a process that is currently running, before that process has voluntarily given it up? Every algorithm in this module answers this question differently, and being able to answer it correctly for each one is exactly what separates a candidate who has memorized names from one who understands mechanics.
2. The Two Definitions, Precisely
Getting these two definitions exactly right matters more than almost anything else in this chapter, because sloppy definitions are where most confusion starts.
Non-preemptive scheduling

In non-preemptive scheduling, once a process starts running on the CPU, it keeps the CPU until it voluntarily gives it up. That release happens in exactly two ways: the process finishes and terminates, or the process blocks itself, typically by issuing an I/O request and waiting for the result. The scheduler is never allowed to forcibly interrupt a process that is currently running. It can only make a new decision at the moment the running process steps aside on its own.
Preemptive scheduling

In preemptive scheduling, the scheduler can forcibly interrupt a running process and take the CPU away from it, even if that process is not finished and never asked to give up the CPU. This typically happens to hand the CPU to a higher priority process or a shorter job. The interrupted process is not killed. Its state is saved, it goes back into the ready queue, and it will resume later from exactly where it left off.

The entire distinction comes down to one moment: does a running process ever lose the CPU against its will? Non-preemptive says never. Preemptive says yes, whenever the scheduler decides something more important has arrived.
3. Classifying Every Algorithm In This Module
blocks.text: 3. Classifying Every Algorithm In This Module

blocks.content: You have already learned the mechanics of five scheduling approaches. Here is exactly where each one lands on the preemptive versus non-preemptive line, and why.

{"headers":["Algorithm","Preemptive or non-preemptive","Why"],"rows":[["FCFS","Non-preemptive","The process that arrives first runs to completion or until it blocks on I/O. The scheduler never interrupts it, no matter how long it runs or what arrives after it."],["SJF (Shortest Job First)","Non-preemptive","The scheduler picks the shortest job available at the moment it chooses, but once that job starts running it keeps the CPU until it finishes, even if a shorter job arrives a moment later."],["SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First)","Preemptive","This is explicitly the preemptive version of SJF. If a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining burst than the process currently running, the scheduler immediately takes the CPU away and gives it to the new arrival."],["Priority Scheduling","Can be either","Both a preemptive variant and a non-preemptive variant genuinely exist and are used in real systems. Which one you get depends entirely on how the scheduler is configured, not on the word priority itself."],["Round Robin","Preemptive","Preemption is built into the design itself through the time quantum. A running process is forcibly interrupted the instant its slice of CPU time expires, regardless of whether it has finished its work."]]}

Two of these deserve a second look. SRTF is not a different algorithm from SJF so much as SJF with permission to change its mind mid execution, which is exactly what makes it preemptive. And Priority Scheduling is the one entry in this table that refuses to sit still: it genuinely has both a preemptive form, where a higher priority arrival interrupts whatever is running, and a non-preemptive form, where the running process is left alone until it finishes or blocks, and the next pick is made only then.
4. When Does a Preemption Actually Happen
blocks.text: 4. When Does a Preemption Actually Happen

blocks.content: Preemptive scheduling is not something that happens randomly or continuously. A preemption is triggered by one of three specific events, and being able to name them precisely is a strong signal of real understanding.

["A timer interrupt fires: the running process has used up its allotted time quantum, most relevant in Round Robin, and the hardware timer forces control back to the scheduler.","A higher priority process arrives in the ready queue: a new process shows up that outranks the one currently running, relevant to preemptive priority scheduling and to SRTF, where a shorter remaining burst counts as higher priority.","A waiting process becomes ready: an I/O operation that a process was blocked on completes, and that process, now ready to run again, turns out to outrank the process currently occupying the CPU."]
items: A timer interrupt fires: the running process has used up its allotted time quantum, most relevant in Round Robin, and the hardware timer forces control back to the scheduler.

A higher priority process arrives in the ready queue: a new process shows up that outranks the one currently running, relevant to preemptive priority scheduling and to SRTF, where a shorter remaining burst counts as higher priority.
A waiting process becomes ready: an I/O operation that a process was blocked on completes, and that process, now ready to run again, turns out to outrank the process currently occupying the CPU.

blocks.content: Why this list matters

Notice that all three events are things the CPU itself cannot decide on its own. A timer interrupt comes from hardware. A new arrival comes from another part of the system creating a process. An I/O completion comes from a device controller. In every case, the running process did nothing wrong and asked for nothing. The interruption is imposed on it entirely from the outside, which is the whole point of the word preemptive.
5. The Real Tradeoffs
Neither approach is simply better. Each one buys real advantages at a real cost, and the cost is different in kind, not just in degree.
Non-preemptive: simple, but it can freeze the system
blocks.text: Non-preemptive: simple, but it can freeze the system

blocks.content: Non-preemptive scheduling is simpler to implement because a running process is never interrupted unexpectedly. There is no risk of a process being caught mid update to a shared data structure, since it is never yanked away in the middle of its own work. The serious downside is responsiveness. A single long running process can hold the CPU for as long as it likes, and every other process, no matter how urgent, simply has to wait its turn. On an interactive system this can make the entire machine feel frozen.
Preemptive: responsive, but genuinely harder to get right
blocks.text: Preemptive: responsive, but genuinely harder to get right

blocks.content: Preemptive scheduling is far better for responsiveness and fairness in an interactive system, because no single process can monopolize the CPU indefinitely. It is essential for real time systems that must meet hard deadlines, since a low priority process can never be allowed to block an urgent one. The cost is real complexity. The scheduler must save and restore process state correctly on every interruption, and because a process can now be paused at literally any point in its execution, there is a genuine risk of race conditions if it was interrupted in the middle of updating data shared with another process.

blocks.title: Forward pointer
blocks.content: That last risk, a process being preempted mid update to shared data and leaving it in an inconsistent state, is exactly the problem the upcoming Synchronization and Concurrency module exists to solve. Preemptive scheduling is precisely what makes synchronization necessary in the first place.
6. A Worked Example: The Same Two Processes, Two Outcomes
blocks.text: 6. A Worked Example: The Same Two Processes, Two Outcomes

blocks.content: The clearest way to see the difference is to run the exact same two processes through both approaches and watch what changes. Process P1 is long, it arrives at time zero with a burst time of eight. Process P2 is short, it arrives at time two with a burst time of two, right while P1 is already running.
{"headers":["Process","Arrival time","Burst time"],"rows":[["P1","0","8"],["P2","2","2"]]}
Under non-preemptive scheduling

P1 is already running when P2 arrives at time two. Because the scheduler cannot forcibly interrupt a running process, P2 simply waits in the ready queue no matter how short it is. P1 keeps the CPU until it finishes at time eight, and only then does P2 get to run.
{"headers":["Process","Completion time","Turnaround time","Waiting time"],"rows":[["P1","8","8","0"],["P2","10","8","6"]]}
Under preemptive scheduling

P1 starts running at time zero as before. At time two, P2 arrives with a burst of two, which is shorter than the six units P1 still has remaining. Because the scheduler is now allowed to preempt, it immediately takes the CPU away from P1 and hands it to P2. P2 runs to completion, and only then does P1 resume with its remaining six units of work.

The total work done is identical in both cases, ten units of CPU time across the same two processes, yet the experience for P2 is completely different. Under non-preemptive scheduling, a two unit job is forced to wait six units simply because it had the misfortune of arriving while something longer was already running. Under preemptive scheduling, that same short job finishes almost immediately, and P1 only pays a small two unit delay for it. This is precisely why SRTF consistently beats SJF on average waiting time, and it is the same underlying reason interactive systems favor preemption despite the added cost of an extra context switch.
7. Why Modern Operating Systems Choose Preemptive Scheduling
blocks.text: 7. Why Modern Operating Systems Choose Preemptive Scheduling

blocks.content: Linux, Windows, and macOS are all built around preemptive multitasking. On a general purpose machine you routinely have dozens of programs competing for the CPU at once, a browser, a music player, a code editor, background sync services, and the operating system itself. Responsiveness is not a nice to have on a system like this, it is the entire point. If any one of those programs could hold the CPU until it felt like giving it back, typing in your editor would freeze every time a background task decided to run.

blocks.title: The pattern to remember
blocks.content: Whenever an operating system genuinely needs to feel responsive to a human sitting in front of it, or needs to guarantee a deadline is met, it reaches for preemptive scheduling. Non-preemptive scheduling survives mainly in older batch systems and in specialized settings where simplicity and predictability matter more than interactivity.
8. Common Misconceptions
A few mistakes come up again and again when people first learn this material, and each one is worth calling out directly.

["Assuming Priority Scheduling is inherently one or the other: it is not. Both a preemptive variant and a non-preemptive variant genuinely exist and are used depending on the system, and you were shown both variants earlier in this module.","Assuming preemption only ever comes from a timer: the timer quantum expiring is only one of three triggers. A higher priority arrival or an I/O completion that wakes up a higher priority process can preempt just as easily, with no timer involved at all.","Assuming non-preemptive scheduling is simply the worse option: it is simpler, more predictable, and carries none of the shared data race risk that preemption introduces, which is exactly why it is still the right choice for certain batch and embedded workloads."]
items: Assuming Priority Scheduling is inherently one or the other: it is not. Both a preemptive variant and a non-preemptive variant genuinely exist and are used depending on the system, and you were shown both variants earlier in this module.

Assuming preemption only ever comes from a timer: the timer quantum expiring is only one of three triggers. A higher priority arrival or an I/O completion that wakes up a higher priority process can preempt just as easily, with no timer involved at all.

Assuming non-preemptive scheduling is simply the worse option: it is simpler, more predictable, and carries none of the shared data race risk that preemption introduces, which is exactly why it is still the right choice for certain batch and embedded workloads.

blocks.content: 9. The Interview Angle

The question "is this algorithm preemptive or non-preemptive" is one of the most common, quickest, and sharpest checks an interviewer can throw at you in an operating systems round. It takes seconds to ask and it is almost impossible to answer correctly by guessing. It immediately reveals whether you actually understand how each algorithm behaves once a process is already running, or whether you only memorized its name and its one line description. Walk in able to classify FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Priority Scheduling, and Round Robin instantly and explain why in one sentence each, and this question stops being something to fear and becomes one of the easiest points you will earn in the entire interview.
